newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bank move may constrain new UK govt - NZ's Brash.
newsitem.headline: Bank move may constrain new UK govt - NZ's Brash.

text.p: Britain's granting of operational independence to the Bank of England may constrain the new government's spending options, Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash said on Wednesday.
Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Tuesday surprised analysts by granting the Bank of England "operational responsibility", modelled on the New Zealand framework.

"It has implications for fiscal policy, clearly," Brash said of the British change. "If government were to embark upon a major expansionary fiscal policy, then monetary policy has to be to that degree somewhat tighter to meet the target which government has set," he told Reuters.
"Governments which directly control both (fiscal and monetary policy) don't like to acknowledge the inflationary implications of what they are doing with fiscal policy."
News that the New Zealand government planned to introduce a tax cut package in 1996 caused the RBNZ to tighten monetary policy because of expected inflationary consequences.

But there have been successes for the New Zealand model, introduced in 1989. Inflation ran in double digits for much of the 1970s and 80s but has been tamed to less than three percent under the current regime.
Brash was loath to say the New Zealand model worked flawlessly, because of breaches of the government-set inflation target band last year.
However, he said the fall in inflation had produced a significant decline in long term inflationary expectations.
Critics say it has also produced the highest real interest rates and an overvalued exchange rate, but Brash said that is not a result of the constitutional framework.

He said one aspect that differentiated the New Zealand model from the Maastricht model was that the government explicitly set the inflation target via a contract signed between the treasurer and the bank governor.
"It simply asks bureaucrats to deliver the will of the elected government.
"I don't think it neuters politicians or governments. On the contrary, it simply makes their role absolutely clear. They retain the right to control," he said.
The new centre-right coalition government in December eased the inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
"There is a great deal to be said for the argument that the choice of the inflation target is a matter which is appropriately determined by elected government," Brash said.
He said it was more democratic that the government was obliged to make its inflation target public.

Brash, who can be fired under his contract for inadequate performance, was unenthusiastic about a British modification to the New Zealand model where a committee sets the official interest rates rather than the central bank governor.
"Clearly, it is more difficult to hold (BoE governor) Eddie George personally accountable when he is simply one member of the committee."
The New Zealand model had delivered lower long-term rates.

"The fact that we have been able to have long-term bond rates lower than Australia and somewhat lower than most parts of the United Kingdom, despite the fact that we are a vastly smaller economy with very large levels of debt traditionally, I think says something about the benefits of the framework."
